Then I asked her, and said, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ And she said, ‘The daughter of Bathual, Nahur’s son, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the nose ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
And I bowed my head and worshiped 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, and Barak the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my master Abraham, who had led me in the way of truth to take the daughter of my master’s brother for his son.
Now if you will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me. And if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left.”
Then Laban and Bathual answered and said, “The thing comes from 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH; we cannot speak to you either bad or good.
Here is Rabakah before you; take her and go, and let her be your master’s son’s wife, as 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has spoken.”
And it came to pass, when Abraham’s servant heard their words, that he worshiped YAHUAH, bowing himself to the Arath.
Then the servant brought out jewelry of silver, jewelry of gold, and clothing, and gave them to Rabakah. He also gave precious things to her brother and to her mother.
And he and the men who were with him ate and drank and stayed all night. Then they arose in the morning, and he said, “Send me away to my master.”
But her brother and her mother said, “Let the young woman stay with us a few days, at least ten; after that she may go.”
And he said to them, “Do not hinder me, since 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has prospered my way; send me away so that I may go to my master.”
So they said, “We will call the young woman and ask her personally.”
Then they called Rabakah and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” And she said, “I will go.”
So they sent away Rabakah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant and his men.
And they Barak Rabakah and said to her: “Our sister, may you becomeThe mother of thousands of ten thousands; And may your descendants possess the gates of those who hate them.”
Then Rabakah and her maids arose, and they rode on the camels and followed the man. So the servant took Rabakah and departed.
Now Yachaq came from the way of Baar Lahai Ruy, for he dwelt in the South.
And Yachaq went out to meditate in the field in the evening; and he lifted his eyes and looked, and there, the camels were coming.
Then Rabakah lifted her eyes, and when she saw Yachaq she dismounted from her camel;
For she had said to the servant, “Who is this man walking in the field to meet us?” The servant said, “It is my master.” So she took a veil and covered herself.
And the servant told Yachaq all the things that he had done.
Then Yachaq brought her into his mother Sharah’s tent; and he took Rabakah and she became his wife, and Yachaq loved Rabakah. So Yachaq was comforted after his mother’s death.
Abraham married another wife, whose name was Katurah.
She gave birth to Zimran, Yukshan, Madan, Midyan, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Yukshan was the father of Shaba and Dadan. Dadan’s descendants were the Asshurites, Latushites, and Laummites.
Midian’s sons were Aphah, Aphar, Hanuch, Abida, and Aldaah. These were all descendants of Abraham through Katurah.
Abraham gave everything he owned to his son Yachaq.
But before he died, he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them off to a land in the east, away from Yachaq.
Abraham lived for one hundred and seventy five years,
And he died at a ripe old age, having lived a long and satisfying life. He breathed his last and joined his ancestors in death.
His sons Yachaq and Ishma'al buried him in the cave of Machpalah, near Mamra, in the field of Aphrun son of Zuhar the Hittite.
This was the field Abraham had purchased from the Hittites and where he had buried his wife Sharah.
After Abraham’s death, 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH Barak his son Yachaq, who settled near Baar-lahay-ruy in the Nagab.
This is the account of the family of Ishma'al, the son of Abraham through Hagar, Sharah’s Mitzraym servant.
Here is a list, by their names and clans, of Ishma'al’s descendants: The oldest was Nabaiuth, followed by Kadar, Adbaal, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tama, Yatur, Naphish, and Kadamah.
These twelve sons of Ishma'al became the founders of twelve tribes named after them, listed according to the places they settled and camped.
Ishma'al lived for 137 years. Then he breathed his last and joined his ancestors in death.
Ishma'al’s descendants occupied the region from Habilah to Shur, which is east of Mitzraym in the direction of Asshur. There they lived in open hostility toward all their relatives.
This is the account of the family of Yachaq, the son of Abraham.
When Yachaq was forty years old, he married Rabakah, the daughter of Bathual the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean.
Yachaq pleaded with 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH on behalf of his wife, because she was unable to have children. 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH answered Yachaq’s prayer, and Rabakah became pregnant with twins.
But the two children struggled with each other in her womb. So she went to ask 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH about it. “Why is this happening to me?” she asked.

And 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH told her, “The sons in your womb will become two nations. From the very beginning, the two nations will be rivals. One nation will be stronger than the other; and your older son will serve your younger son.”
And when the time came to give birth, Rabakah discovered that she did indeed have twins!
The first one was very red at birth and covered with thick hair like a fur coat. So they named him Asau.
Then the other twin was born with his hand grasping Asau’s heel. So they named him Ya'aqub. Yachaq was sixty years old when the twins were born.
As the boys grew up, Asau became a skillful hunter. He was an outdoorsman, but Ya'aqub had a quiet temperament, preferring to stay at home.
Yachaq loved Asau because he enjoyed eating the wild game Asau brought home, but Rabakah loved Ya'aqub.
One day when Ya'aqub was cooking some stew, Asau arrived home from the wilderness exhausted and hungry.
Asau said to Ya'aqub, “I am starved! Give me some of that red stew!” (This is how Asau got his other name, Adum, which means “red.”)
“All right,” Ya'aqub replied, “but trade me your rights as the firstborn son.”
“Look, I’m dying of starvation!” said Asau. “What good is my birthright to me now?”
But Ya'aqub said, “First you must swear that your birthright is mine.” So Asau swore an oath, thereby selling all his rights as the firstborn to his brother, Ya'aqub.
Then Ya'aqub gave Asau some bread and lentil stew. Asau ate the meal, then got up and left. Thus Asau despised his birthright.
A severe famine now struck the land, as had happened before in Abraham’s time. So Yachaq moved to Garar, where Abimalach, king of the Philistines, lived.
For YAHUAH appeared to Yachaq and said, “Do not go down to Mitzraym, but do as I tell you.

Live here as a foreigner in this land, and I will be with you and barak you. I hereby confirm that I will give all these lands to you and your descendants, just as I solemnly promised Abraham, your father.
I will cause your descendants to become as numerous as the stars of the sky, and I will give them all these lands. And through your descendants all the nations of the Arath (earth) will be barak.
I will do this because Abraham listened to me and obeyed all my requirements, commands, decrees, and instructions.”
So Yachaq stayed in Garar.

When the men who lived there asked Yachaq about his wife, Rabakah, he said, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to say, “She is my wife.” He thought, “They will kill me to get her, because she is so beautiful.”
But some time later, Abimalach, king of the Philistines, looked out his window and saw Yachaq caressing Rabakah.

Immediately, Abimalach called for Yachaq and exclaimed, “She is obviously your wife! Why did you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Yachaq replied, “Because I was afraid someone would kill me to get her from me.
“How could you do this to us?” Abimalach exclaimed. “One of my people might easily have taken your wife and slept with her, and you would have made us guilty of great sin.”
Then Abimalach issued a public proclamation: “Anyone who touches this man or his wife will be put to death!”
When Yachaq planted his crops that year, he harvested a hundred times more grain than he planted, for 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH baraked him.
He became a very rich man, and his wealth continued to grow.
He acquired so many flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, and servants that the Philistines became jealous of him.
So the Philistines filled up all of Yachaq’s wells with dirt. These were the wells that had been dug by the servants of his father, Abraham.
Finally, Abimalach ordered Yachaq to leave the country. “Go somewhere else,” he said, “for you have become too powerful for us.”
So Yachaq moved away to the Garar Valley, where he set up their tents and settled down.
He reopened the wells his father had dug, which the Philistines had filled in after Abraham’s death. Yachaq also restored the names Abraham had given them.
Yachaq’s servants also dug in the Garar Valley and discovered a well of fresh water.
But then the shepherds from Garar came and claimed the spring. “This is our water,” they said, and they argued over it with Yachaq’s herdsmen. So Yachaq named the well Asak (which means “argument”).
Yachaq’s men then dug another well, but again there was a dispute over it. So Yachaq named it Sitnah (which means “hostility”).

Abandoning that one, Yachaq moved on and dug another well. This time there was no dispute over it, so Yachaq named the place Rahubuth (which means “open space”), for he said, “At last 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has created enough space for us to prosper in this land.”
From there Yachaq moved to Baarshaba,

There 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH appeared to him on the night of his arrival. “I AM the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of your father, Abraham, Do not be afraid, for I am with you and I will barak you. I will multiply your descendants, and they will become a great nation. I will do this because of my promise to Abraham, my servant.”
Then Yachaq built an altar there and worshiped 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH. He set up his camp at that place, and his servants dug another well.
One day King Abimalach came from Gerar with his adviser, Ahuzzath, and also Phicul, his army commander.
“Why have you come here?” Yachaq asked. “You obviously hate me, since you kicked me off your land.”
They replied, “We can plainly see that 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH is with you. So we want to enter into a sworn treaty with you. Let’s make a covenant.
Swear that you will not harm us, just as we have never troubled you. We have always treated you well, and we sent you away from us in Shalum. And now look how 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has Baraked you!”
So Yachaq prepared a covenant feast to celebrate the treaty, and they ate and drank together.
Early the next morning, they each took a solemn oath not to interfere with each other. Then Yachaq sent them home again, and they left him in Shalum.
That very day Yachaq’s servants came and told him about a new well they had dug. “We have found water!” they exclaimed.
So Yachaq named the well Shibah (which means “oath”). And to this day the town that grew up there is called Baarshaba (which means “well of the oath”).
At the age of forty, Asau married two Hittite wives: Yudith, the daughter of Baari, and Basamath, the daughter of Alun.
But Asau’s wives made life miserable for Yachaq and Rabakah.
Now Yachaq was old and turning blind, he called for Asau, his older son, and said, “My son. “Yes, Father?” Asau replied.
“I am an old man now,” Yachaq said, “and I do not know the day of my death.
Take your bow and a quiver full of arrows, and go out into the open country to hunt some wild game for me.
Prepare my favorite dish, and bring it here for me to eat. Then I will pronounce the Barakah that belongs to you, my firstborn son, before I die.”
But Rabakah overheard what Yachaq had said to his son Asau. So when Asau left to hunt for the wild game,
Rabakah said to her son Ya'aqub, “Listen. I overheard your father say to Asau,
‘Bring me some wild game and prepare me a delicious meal. Then I will barak you in 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH’s presence before I die.’
Now, my son, listen to me. Do exactly as I tell you.
Go out to the flocks, and bring me two fine young goats. I will use them to prepare your father’s favorite dish.
Then take the food to your father so he can eat it and barak you before he dies.”
“But look,” Ya'aqub replied to his mother, “my brother, Asau, is a hairy man, and my skin is smooth.
What if my father touches me? He will see that I am trying to trick him, and then he will curse me instead of Barakah.”
And his mother replied, “Then let the curse fall on me, my son! Just do what I tell you. Go out and get the goats for me!”
So Ya'aqub went out and got the young goats for his mother. Rabakah took them and prepared a delicious meal, just the way Yachaq liked it.
Then she took Asau’s favorite clothes, which were there in the house, and gave them to her younger son, Ya'aqub.
She covered his arms and the smooth part of his neck with the skin of the young goats.
Then she gave Ya'aqub the delicious meal, including freshly baked bread.
So Ya'aqub took the food to his father. “My father?” he said. “Yes, my son,” Yachaq answered. “Who are you, Asau or Ya'aqub?”
Ya'aqub replied, “It’s Asau, your firstborn son. I have done as you told me. Here is the wild game. Now sit up and eat it so you can give me your Barakah.”
Yachaq asked, “How did you find it so quickly, my son?” 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH put it in my path!” Ya'aqub replied.
Then Yachaq said to Ya'aqub, “Come closer so I can touch you and make sure that you really are Asau.”
So Ya'aqub went closer to his father, and Yachaq touched him and said, the voice is Ya'aqub’s, but the hands are Asau’s.
But Yachaq did not recognize Ya'aqub, because Ya'aqub’s hands felt hairy just like Asau’s. So Yachaq prepared to barak Ya'aqub.
“But are you really my son Asau?” Yachaq asked. “Yes, I am,” Ya'aqub replied.

Then Yachaq said, “Now, my son, bring me the wild game. Let me eat it, and then I will give you my Barakah.” So Ya'aqub took the food to his father, and Yachaq ate it. He also drank the wine that Ya'aqub served him.
Then Yachaq said to Ya'aqub, “Please come a little closer and kiss me, my son.”

So Ya'aqub went over and kissed him. And when Yachaq caught the smell of his clothes, he was finally convinced, and he barak his son, he said, “Ah! The smell of my son is like the smell of the outdoors, which 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has Baraked!
“From the dew of Shamaym and the richness of the Arath (earth), may 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH always give you abundant harvests of grain and bountiful new wine.

May many nations become your servants, and may they bow down to you. May you be the master over your brothers, and may your mother’s sons bow down to you. All who curse you will be cursed, and all who barak you will be Baraked.”
As soon as Yachaq had finished the Barakah to Ya'aqub, and almost before Ya'aqub had left his father, Asau returned from his hunt.
Asau prepared a delicious meal and brought it to his father. Then he said, “Sit up, my father, and eat my wild game so you can give me your Barakah.”
But Yachaq asked him, “Who are you?” Asau replied, “It’s your son, your firstborn son, Asau.”
Yachaq began to tremble uncontrollably and said, “Then who just served me wild game? I have already eaten it, and I baraked him just before you came. And yes, that Barakah must stand!”
When Asau heard his father’s words, he let out a loud and bitter cry. “Oh my father, what about me? Barak me, too!” he begged.
But Yachaq said, “Your brother was here, and he tricked me, he has taken away your Barakah.”

Asau exclaimed, “No wonder his name is Ya'aqub, for now he has cheated me twice, first he took my rights as the firstborn, and now he has stolen my Barakah. Oh, haven’t you saved even one Barakah for me?”

Yachaq said to Asau, “I have made Ya'aqub your master and have declared that all his brothers will be his servants. I have guaranteed him an abundance of grain and wine, what is left for me to give you, my son?”
Asau pleaded, “But do you have only one Barakah? Oh my father, barak me, too!” Then Asau broke down and wept.
Finally, his father, Yachaq, said to him, “You will live away from the richness of the Arath (earth), and away from the dew of the Shamaym above.
You will live by your sword, and you will serve your brother. But when you decide to break free, you will shake his yoke from your neck.”
From that time on, Asau hated Ya'aqub because their father had given Ya'aqub the Barakah. And Asau began to scheme: “I will soon be mourning my father’s death. Then I will kill my brother, Ya'aqub.”
But Rabakah heard about Asau’s plans. So she sent for Ya'aqub and told him, “Listen, Asau is consoling himself by plotting to kill you.
So listen carefully, my son. Get ready and flee to my brother, Laban, in Haran.
Stay there with him until your brother cools off.
When he calms down and forgets what you have done to him, I will send for you to come back. Why should I lose both of you in one day?”
Then Rabakah said to Yachaq, “I’m sick and tired of these local Hittite women! I would rather die than see Ya'aqub marry one of them.”
Then Yachaq called Ya'aqub and Baraked him, and charged him, and said to him: “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
Arise, go to Padan Aram, to the house of Bathual your mother’s father; and take yourself a wife from there of the daughters of Laban your mother’s brother.
“May 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH (AL'Mighty ONE) Barak you, And make you fruitful and multiply you, That you may be an assembly of multitude;
And give to you the Barakah of Abraham, and your descendants with you, that you may inherit the land in which you are a stranger, Which 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH gave to Abraham.”
So Yachaq sent Ya'aqub away, and he went to Padan Aram, to Laban the son of Bathual, the brother of Rabakah, the mother of Ya'aqub and Asau.

Asau saw that Yachaq had Baraked Ya'aqub and sent him away to Padan Aram to take himself a wife from there, and that as he Baraked him he gave him a charge, saying, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan,”
And that Ya'aqub had obeyed his father and his mother and had gone to Padan Aram.
Also Asau saw that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father Yachaq.
So Asau went to Ishma'al and took Mahalath the daughter of Ishma'al, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nabayuth, to be his wife in addition to the wives he had.
Now Ya'aqub went out from Baarshaba and went toward Haran.
So he came to a certain place and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. And he took one of the stones of that place and put it at his head, and he lay down in that place to sleep.
Then he dreamed, and behold, a ladder was set up on the Arath (earth), and its top reached to Shamaym; and there the Malakym of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH were ascending and descending on it.
And behold, 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH stood above it and said: “I AM the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of Abraham your father and the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of Yachaq; the land on which you lie I will give to you and your descendants.

Also your descendants shall be as the dust of the Arath (earth); you shall spread abroad to the west and the east, to the north and the south; and in you and in your seed all the families of the Arath shall be Baraked.
Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land; for I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you.”
Then Ya'aqub awoke from his sleep and said, “Surely 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH is in this place, and I did not know it.”
And he was afraid and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, and this is the gate of Shamaym!”
Then Ya'aqub rose early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put at his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on top of it.
And he called the name of that place Bathal; but the name of that city had been Luz previously.
Then Ya'aqub made a vow, saying, “If 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH will be with me, and keep me in this way that I am going, and give me bread to eat and clothing to put on,
So that I come back to my father’s house in Shalum, then 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH shall be my 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH.
And this stone which I have set as a pillar shall be 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH’s house, and of all that You give me I will surely give a tenth to You.”
Now Ya'aqub went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the East.
And he looked, and saw a well in the field; and behold, there were three flocks of sheep lying by it; for out of that well they watered the flocks. A large stone was on the well’s mouth.
Now all the flocks would be gathered there; and they would roll the stone from the well’s mouth, water the sheep and put the stone back in its place on the well’s mouth.
And Ya'aqub said to them, “My brethren, where are you from?” And they said, “We are from Haran.”
Then he said to them, “Do you know Laban the son of Nahur?” And they said, “We know him.”
So he said to them, “Is he well?” And they said, “He is well. And look, his daughter Rach'al is coming with the sheep.”
Then he said, “Look, it is still high day; it is not time for the cattle to be gathered together. Water the sheep, and go and feed them.”
But they said, “We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together, and they have rolled the stone from the well’s mouth; then we water the sheep.”
Now while Ya'aqub was still speaking with them, Rach'al came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

And it came to pass, when Ya'aqub saw Rach'al the daughter of Laban his mother’s brother, and his sheep, Ya'aqub went near and rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his uncle.
Then Ya'aqub kissed Rach'al, and lifted up his voice and wept.
And Ya'aqub told Rach'al that he was her father’s relative and that he was Rabakah’s son. So she ran and told her father.

Then it came to pass, when Laban heard the report about Ya'aqub his sister’s son, that he ran to meet him, and embraced him and kissed him, and brought him to his house. So he told Laban all these things.
And Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” And he stayed with him for a month.
Then Laban said to Ya'aqub, “Because you are my relative, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what should your wages be?”
Now Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was La'ah, and the name of the younger was Rach'al.
La'ah’s eyes were delicate, but Rach'al was beautiful of form and appearance.
Now Ya'aqub loved Rach'al; so he said, “I will serve you seven years for Rach'al your younger daughter.”
And Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to another man. Stay with me.”
So Ya'aqub served seven years for Rach'al, and they seemed only a few days to him because of the love he had for her.
Then Ya'aqub said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.”
And Laban gathered together all the men of the place and made a feast.
Now it came to pass in the evening, that he took La'ah his daughter and brought her to Ya'aqub; and he went in to her.
And Laban gave his maid Zilpah to his daughter La'ah as a maid.
So it came to pass in the morning, that behold, it was La'ah. And Ya'aqub said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Was it not for Rach'al that I served you? Why then have you deceived me?”
And Laban said, “It must not be done so in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn.
Fulfill her week, and we will give you this one also for the service which you will serve with me still another seven years.”
Then Ya'aqub did so and fulfilled her week. So he gave him his daughter Rach'al as wife also.
And Laban gave his maid Bilhah to his daughter Rach'al as a maid.
Then Ya'aqub also went in to Rach'al, and he also loved Rach'al more than La'ah. And he served with Laban still another seven years.
When 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH saw that La'ah was unloved, HE opened her womb; but Rach'al was barren.
So La'ah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Rauban; for she said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has surely looked on my affliction. Now therefore, my husband will love me.”
Then she conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Because 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has heard that I am unloved, He has therefore given me this son also.” And she called his name Shimun.
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Now this time my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Lauy.
And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Now I will Yadah YAHUAH. Therefore she called his name Yahudah. Then she stopped bearing.
When Rach'al saw that she wasn’t having any children for Ya'aqub, she became jealous of her sister. She pleaded with Ya'aqub, “Give me children, or I will die!”
Then Ya'aqub became furious with Rach'al. “Am I 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH?” he asked. “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH is the one who has kept you from having children!”
Then Rach'al told him, “Take my maid, Bilh'ah, and sleep with her. She will bear children for me, and through her I can have a family, too.”
So Rach'al gave her servant, Bilh'ah, to Ya'aqub as a wife, and he slept with her.
Bilh'ah became pregnant and presented him with a son.
Rach'al named him Dan, for she said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has vindicated me! He has heard my request and given me a son.”
Then Bilh'ah became pregnant again and gave Ya'aqub a second son.
Rach'al named him Naphtaly, for she said, “I have struggled hard with my sister, and I am winning!”
Meanwhile, La'ah realized that she wasn’t getting pregnant anymore, so she took her servant, Zilp'ah, and gave her to Ya'aqub as a wife.
Soon Zilp'ah presented him with a son.
La'ah named him Gad, for she said, “How fortunate I am!”
Then Zilp'ah gave Ya'aqub a second son.
And La'ah named him Ashar, for she said, “The joy is mine! Now the other women will celebrate with me.”
One day during the wheat harvest, Rauban found some mandrakes growing in a field and brought them to his mother, La'ah. Rach'al begged La'ah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

But La'ah angrily replied, “Was it not enough that you stole my husband? Now will you steal my son’s mandrakes, too?” Rachal answered, “I will let Ya'aqub sleep with you tonight if you give me some of the mandrakes.”

So that evening, as Ya'aqub was coming home from the fields, La'ah went out to meet him. “You must come and sleep with me tonight!” she said. “I have paid for you with some mandrakes that my son found.” So that night Ya'aqub slept with La'ah.
And 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH answered La'ah’s prayers. She became pregnant again and gave birth to a fifth son for Ya'aqub.
She named him Issachar, for she said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has rewarded me for giving my servant to my husband as a wife.”
Then La'ah became pregnant again and gave birth to a sixth son for Ya'aqub.
She named him Zabulun, for she said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has given me a good reward. Now my husband will treat me with respect, for I have given him six sons.”
Later she gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH remembered Rach'al’s plight and answered her prayers by enabling her to have children.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, and she said “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has removed me from shame,.
And she named him Ya'asaf, for she said, “May 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH add yet another son to my family.”
Soon after Rach'al had given birth to Ya'asaf, Ya'aqub said to Laban, “Please release me so I can go home to my own country.
Let me take my wives and children, for I have earned them by serving you, and let me be on my way. You certainly know how hard I have worked for you.”
“Please listen to me,” Laban replied. “I have become wealthy, for 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has Baraked me because of you.
Tell me how much I owe you. Whatever it is, I will pay it.”
Ya'aqub replied, “You know how hard I’ve worked for you, and how your flocks and herds have grown under my care.

You had little indeed before I came, but your wealth has increased enormously. 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has Baraked you through everything I have done. But now, what about me? When can I start providing for my own family?”
“What wages do you want?” Laban asked again. Ya'aqub replied, “Don’t give me anything. Just do this one thing, and I will continue to tend and watch over your flocks.
Let me inspect your flocks today and remove all the sheep and goats that are speckled or spotted, along with all the black sheep. Give these to me as my wages.

In the future, when you check on the animals you have given me as my wages, you’ll see that I have been honest. If you find in my flock any goats without speckles or spots, or any sheep that are not black, you will know that I have stolen them from you.”
“All right,” Laban replied. “It will be as you say.”

But that very day Laban went out and removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted, all the female goats that were speckled and spotted or had white patches, and all the black sheep. He placed them in the care of his own sons,
Who took them a three-days’ journey from where Ya'aqub was. Meanwhile, Ya'aqub stayed and cared for the rest of Laban’s flock.
Then Ya'aqub took some fresh branches from poplar, almond, and plane trees and peeled off strips of bark, making white streaks on them.
Then he placed these peeled branches in the watering troughs where the flocks came to drink, for that was where they mated.
And when they mated in front of the white-streaked branches, they gave birth to young that were streaked, speckled, and spotted.

Ya'aqub separated those lambs from Laban’s flock. And at mating time he turned the flock to face Laban’s animals that were streaked or black. This is how he built his own flock instead of increasing Laban’s.
Whenever the stronger females were ready to mate, Ya'aqub would place the peeled branches in the watering troughs in front of them. Then they would mate in front of the branches.
But Ya'aqub did not do this with the weaker ones, so the weaker lambs belonged to Laban, and the stronger ones were Ya'aqub’s.
As a result, Ya'aqub became very wealthy, with large flocks of sheep and goats, female and male servants, and many camels and donkeys.
But Ya'aqub soon learned that Laban’s sons were grumbling about him. Ya'aqub has robbed our father of everything!” they said. “He has gained all his wealth at our father’s expense.”
And Ya'aqub began to notice a change in Laban’s attitude toward him.
Then 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH said to Ya'aqub, “Return to the land of your father and grandfather and to your relatives there, and I will be with you.”
So Ya'aqub called Rach'al and La'ah out to the field where he was watching his flock.
He said to them, “I have noticed that your father’s attitude toward me has changed. But the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my father has been with me.
You know how hard I have worked for your father,
But he has cheated me, changing my wages ten times. But 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has not allowed him to do me any harm.

For if he said, ‘The speckled animals will be your wages,’ the whole flock began to produce speckled young. And when he changed his mind and said, ‘The striped animals will be your wages,’ then the whole flock produced striped young.
In this way, 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has taken your father’s animals and given them to me.
“One time during the mating season, I had a dream and saw that the male goats mating with the females were streaked, speckled, and spotted.
Then in my dream, the Malak of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH said to me, Ya'aqub!’ And I replied, ‘Yes, here I am.’
“The Malak said, ‘Look up, and you will see that only the streaked, speckled, and spotted males are mating with the females of your flock. For I have seen how Laban has treated you.

I AM the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH who appeared to you at Bath'al, the place where you anointed the pillar of stone and made your vow to me. Now get ready and leave this country and return to the land of your birth.’”
Rach'al and La'ah responded, “That’s fine with us! We won’t inherit any of our father’s wealth anyway.
He has reduced our rights to those of foreign women. And after he sold us, he wasted the money you paid him for us.
All the wealth 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has given you from our father legally belongs to us and our children. So go ahead and do whatever 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has told you.”
So Ya'aqub put his wives and children on camels,
And he drove all his livestock in front of him. He packed all the belongings he had acquired in Paddan-aram and set out for the land of Canaan, where his father, Yachaq, lived.
At the time they left, Laban was some distance away, shearing his sheep. Rach'al stole her father’s household idols and took them with her.
Ya'aqub outwitted Laban the Aramean, for they set out secretly and never told Laban they were leaving.
So Ya'aqub took all his possessions with him and crossed the Euphrates River, heading for the hill country of Gilaad.
Three days later, Laban was told that Ya'aqub had fled.
So he gathered a group of his relatives and set out in hot pursuit. He caught up with Ya'aqub seven days later in the hill country of Gilaad.
But the previous night 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH had appeared to Laban the Aramean in a dream and told him, “I AM warning you—leave Ya'aqub alone!”
Laban caught up with Ya'aqub as he was camped in the hill country of Gilaad, and he set up his camp not far from Ya'aqub’s.
“What do you mean by deceiving me like this?” Laban demanded. “How dare you drag my daughters away like prisoners of war?

Why did you slip away secretly? Why did you deceive me? And why did you not say you wanted to leave? I would have given you a farewell feast, with singing and music, accompanied by tambourines and harps.
Why did you not let me kiss my daughters and grandchildren and tell them good-bye? You have acted very foolishly!
I could destroy you, but the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of your father appeared to me last night and warned me, ‘Leave Ya'aqub alone!’
I can understand your feeling that you must go, and your intense longing for your father’s home. But why have you stolen my idols?”
“I rushed away because I was afraid,” Ya'aqub answered. “I thought you would take your daughters from me by force.

But as for your idols, see if you can find them, and let the person who has taken them die! And if you find anything else that belongs to you, identify it before all these relatives of ours, and I will give it back!” But Ya'aqub did not know that Rach'al had stolen the household idols.
Laban went first into Ya'aqub’s tent to search there, then into La'ah’s, and then the tents of the two servant wives—but he found nothing. Finally, he went into Rach'al’s tent.
For Rach'al had taken the household idols and hidden them in her camel saddle, and now she was sitting on them. When Laban had thoroughly searched her tent without finding them,
She said to her father, “Please, sir, forgive me if I do not get up for you. I am having my monthly period.” So Laban continued his search, but he could not find the household idols.
Then Ya'aqub became very angry, and he challenged Laban. “What is my crime?” he demanded. “What have I done wrong to make you chase after me as though I were a criminal?
You have rummaged through everything I own. Now show me what you found that belongs to you! Set it out here in front of us, before our relatives, for all to see. Let them judge between us!
“For twenty years I have been with you, caring for your flocks. In all that time your sheep and goats never miscarried. In all those years I never used a single ram of yours for food.

If any were attacked and killed by wild animals, I never showed you the carcass and asked you to reduce the count of your flock. No, I took the loss myself! You made me pay for every stolen animal, whether it was taken in broad daylight or in the dark of night.
“I worked for you through the scorching heat of the day and through cold and sleepless nights.
Yes, for twenty years I slaved in your house! I worked for fourteen years earning your two daughters, and then six more years for your flock. And you changed my wages ten times!

In fact, if the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my father had not been on my side—the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of Abraham and the fearsome 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of Yachaq, you would have sent me away empty-handed. But 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has seen your abuse and my hard work. That is why he appeared to you last night and rebuked you!”

Then Laban replied to Ya'aqub, “These women are my daughters, these children are my grandchildren, and these flocks are my flocks—in fact, everything you see is mine. But what can I do now about my daughters and their children?
So come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and it will be a witness to our commitment.”
So Ya'aqub took a stone and set it up as a monument.
Then he told his family members, “Gather some stones.” So they gathered stones and piled them in a heap. Then Ya'aqub and Laban sat down beside the pile of stones to eat a covenant meal.
To commemorate the event, Laban called the place Yagar-sahadutha (which means “witness pile” in Aramaic), and called it Galaad (which means “witness pile” in Abary_Hebrew).
Then Laban declared, “This pile of stones will stand as a witness to remind us of the covenant we have made today.” This explains why it was called Galaad—“Witness Pile.”
But it was also called Mizpah (which means “watchtower”), for Laban said, “May 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH keep watch between us to make sure that we keep this covenant when we are out of each other’s sight.
If you mistreat my daughters or if you marry other wives, 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH will see it even if no one else does. HE is a witness to this covenant between us.
“See this pile of stones,” Laban continued, “and see this monument I have set between us.
They stand between us as witnesses of our vows. I will never pass this pile of stones to harm you, and you must never pass these stones or this monument to harm me.

I call on the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of our ancestors, the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of your grandfather Abraham and the 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my grandfather Nahur to serve as a judge between us.” So Ya'aqub took an oath before the fearsome 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of his father, Yachaq, to respect the boundary line.
Then Ya'aqub offered a sacrifice to 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH there on the mountain and invited everyone to a covenant feast. After they had eaten, they spent the night on the mountain.
Laban got up early the next morning, and he kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and Baraked them. Then he left and returned home.
As Ya'aqub started on his way again, the Malak of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH came to meet him.
When Ya'aqub saw them, he exclaimed, “This is 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH’s camp!” So he named the place Mahanaim.
Then Ya'aqub sent messengers ahead to his brother, Asau, who was living in the region of Sair in the land of Adum.
He told them, “Give this message to my master Asau: ‘Humble greetings from your servant Ya'aqub. Until now I have been living with Uncle Laban,

And now I own cattle, donkeys, flocks of sheep and goats, and many servants, both men and women. I have sent these messengers to inform my master of my coming, hoping that you will be friendly to me.’”
After delivering the message, the messengers returned to Ya'aqub and reported, “We met your brother, Asau, and he is already on his way to meet you—with an army of 400 men!”
Ya'aqub was terrified at the news, he divided his household, along with the flocks and herds and camels, into two groups.
He thought, “If Asau meets one group and attacks it, perhaps the other group can escape.”

Then Ya'aqub prayed, “O 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my grandfather Abraham, and 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH of my father Yachaq, O 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, you told me, ‘Return to your own land and to your relatives.’ And You promised me that You will treat me kindly.’

I am not worthy of all the unfailing love and faithfulness you have shown to me, your servant. When I left home and crossed the Yurdan River, I owned nothing except a walking stick. Now my household fills two large camps!
O 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, please rescue me from the hand of my brother, Asau. I am afraid that he is coming to attack me, along with my wives and children.
But you promised me, ‘You will surely treat me kindly, and You will multiply my descendants until they become as numerous as the sands along the seashore, too many to count.’”
Ya'aqub stayed where he was for the night. Then he selected these gifts from his possessions to present to his brother, Asau:
Two hundred female goats, twenty male goats, two hundred ewes, twenty rams,
Thirty female camels with their young, 40 cows, 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys, and 10 male donkeys.
He divided these animals into herds and assigned each to different servants. Then he told his servants, “Go ahead of me with the animals, but keep some distance between the herds.”
He gave these instructions to the men leading the first group: “When my brother, Asau, meets you, he will ask, ‘Whose servants are you? Where are you going? Who owns these animals?’
You must reply, ‘They belong to your servant Ya'aqub, but they are a gift for his master Asau. Look, he is coming right behind us.’”
Ya'aqub gave the same instructions to the second and third herdsmen and to all who followed behind the herds: “You must say the same thing to Asau when you meet him.

And be sure to say, ‘Look, your servant Ya'aqub is right behind us.’ Ya'aqub thought, “I will try to appease him by sending gifts ahead of me. When I see him in person, perhaps he will be friendly to me.”
So the gifts were sent on ahead, while Ya'aqub himself spent that night in the camp.
During the night Ya'aqub got up and took his two wives, his two servant wives, and his eleven sons and crossed the Yaabbuk River with them.
After taking them to the other side, he sent over all his possessions.
This left Ya'aqub all alone in the camp, and a man came and wrestled with him until the dawn began to break.
When the man saw that he would not win the match, he touched Ya'aqub’s hip and wrenched it out of its socket.
Then the man said, “Let me go, for the dawn is breaking!” But Ya'aqub said, “I will not let you go unless you Barak me.”
“And the man asked, What is your name?” and he replied, my name is Ya'aqub.
“Your name will no longer be Ya'aqub,” the man told him. “From now on you will be called YASHAR'AL, because you have fought with 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH and with men and have won.”
“Please tell me your name,” Ya'aqub said. “Why do you want to know my name?” the man replied. Then he Baraked Ya'aqub there.
Ya'aqub named the place Pani'AL (which means “face of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH”), for he said, “I have seen 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH face to face, yet my life has been spared.”
The sun was rising as Ya'aqub left Pani'AL, and he was limping because of the injury to his hip.
(Even today the people of YASHAR'AL don’t eat the tendon near the hip socket because of what happened that night when the man strained the tendon of Ya'aqub’s hip).
Then Ya'aqub looked up and saw Asau coming with his 400 men. So he divided the children among La'ah, Rach'al, and his two servant wives.
He put the servant wives and their children at the front, La'ah and her children next, and Rach'al and Ya'asaf last.
Then Ya'aqub went on ahead. As he approached his brother, he bowed to the ground seven times before him.
Then Asau ran to meet him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept.
Then Asau looked at the women and children and asked, “Who are these people with you?” These are the children 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has given to me, your servant,” Ya'aqub replied.
Then the servant wives came forward with their children and bowed before him.
Next came La'ah with her children, and they bowed before him. Finally, Ya'asaf and Rach'al came forward and bowed before him.
“And what were all the flocks and herds I met as I came?” Asau asked. Ya'aqub replied, “They are a gift, my master, to ensure your friendship.”
“My brother, I have plenty,” Asau answered. “Keep what you have for yourself.”
But Ya'aqub insisted, “No, if I have found favor with you, please accept this gift from me. And what a relief to see your friendly smile. It is like seeing the face of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH!
Please take this gift I have brought you, for 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has been very gracious to me. I have more than enough.” And because Ya'aqub insisted, Asau finally accepted the gift.
“Well,” Asau said, “let us be going. I will lead the way.”

But Ya'aqub replied, “You can see, my master, that some of the children are very young, and the flocks and herds have their young, too. If they are driven too hard, even for one day, all the animals could die.
Please, my master, go ahead of your servant. We will follow slowly, at a pace that is comfortable for the livestock and the children. I will meet you at Sair.”
“All right,” Asau said, “but at least let me assign some of my men to guide and protect you.” Ya'aqub responded, “That’s not necessary. It’s enough that you have received me warmly, my master!”
So Asau turned around and started back to Sair that same day.
Ya'aqub, on the other hand, traveled on to Succuth. There he built himself a house and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place was named Succuth (which means “shelters”).
Later, having traveled all the way from Paddan-aram, Ya'aqub arrived safely at the town of Shacham, in the land of Canaan. There he set up camp outside the town.
Ya'aqub bought the plot of land where he camped from the family of Hamur, the father of Shacham, for 100 pieces of silver.
And there he built an altar and named it AL'Aluha-Yashar'al.
Now Dinah the daughter of La'ah, whom she had borne to Ya'aqub, went out to see the daughters of the land.
And when Shacham the son of Hamur the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her and lay with her, and violated her.
His soul was strongly attracted to Dinah the daughter of Ya'aqub, and he loved the young woman and spoke kindly to the young woman.
So Shacham spoke to his father Hamur, saying, “Get me this young woman as a wife.”
And Ya'aqub heard that he had defiled Dinah his daughter. Now his sons were with his livestock in the field; so Ya'aqub held his Shalum until they came.
Then Hamur the father of Shacham went out to Ya'aqub to speak with him.

And the sons of Ya'aqub came in from the field when they heard it; and the men were grieved and very angry, because he had done a shameful thing in YASHAR'AL by sleeping with Ya'aqub’s daughter, a thing which ought not to be done.
But Hamur spoke with them, saying, “The soul of my son Shacham longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as a wife.
And make marriages with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters to yourselves.
So you shall dwell with us, and the land shall be before you. Dwell and trade in it, and acquire possessions for yourselves in it.”
Then Shacham said to her father and her brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give.
Ask me ever so much dowry and gift, and I will give according to what you say to me; but give me the young woman as a wife.”
But the sons of Ya'aqub answered Shacham and Hamur his father, and spoke deceitfully, because he had defiled Dinah their sister.
And they said to them, “We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised, for that would be a reproach to us.
But on this condition we will consent to you: If you will become as we are, if every male of you is circumcised,
Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to us; and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people.
But if you will not heed us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter and be gone.”
And their words pleased Hamur and Shacham, Hamur’s son.
So the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Ya'aqub’s daughter, he was more honorable than all the household of his father.
And Hamur and Shacham his son came to the gate of their city, and spoke with the men of their city, saying:

“These men are at Shalum with us. Therefore let them dwell in the land and trade in it. For indeed the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters to us as wives, and let us give them our daughters.
Only on this condition will the men consent to dwell with us, to be one people: if every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised.
If we do this, their livestock, their property, and every animal of theirs will be ours, Only let us consent to them, and they will dwell with us.”
And all who went out of the gate of his city heeded Hamur and Shacham his son; every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.

Now it came to pass on the third day, when they were in pain, that two of the sons of Ya'aqub, Shimun and Lauy, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword and came boldly upon the city and killed all the males.
And they killed Hamur and Shacham his son with the edge of the sword, and took Dinah from Shacham’s house, and went out.
The sons of Ya'aqub came upon the slain, and plundered the city, because their sister had been defiled.
They took their sheep, their oxen, and their donkeys, what was in the city and what was in the field,
And all their wealth, all their little ones and their wives they took captive; and they plundered even all that was in the houses.

Then Ya'aqub said to Shimun and Lauy, “You have troubled me by making me obnoxious among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Parizzites; and since I am few in number, they will gather themselves together against me and kill me. I and my household shall be destroyed.”
But they said, “Should he treat our sister like a harlot?”
Then 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH Dabar to Ya'aqub, Arise, go up to Bathal, and dwell there: and make there an altar to 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, that appeared to you when you fled from the face of Asau your brother.
Then Ya'aqub said to his household, and to all that were with him, Put away the strange idols that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments:
And let us arise, and go up to Bathal; and I will make there an altar unto 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me in the way which I went.
And they gave unto Ya'aqub all the strange idols which were in their hand, and all their earrings which were in their ears; and Ya'aqub hid them under the oak which was by Shacham.
And they journeyed: and the terror of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was upon the cities that were round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Ya'aqub.
So Ya'aqub came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, that is, Bathal, he and all the people that were with him.
And he built there an altar, and called the place Albathal: because there 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother.
Then Daburah, Rabakah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Bathal under an oak: and the name of it was called Allunbachuth.
And 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH appeared unto Ya'aqub again, when he came out of Padanaram, and Baraked him.
And 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH Dabar unto Ya'aqub, your name is Ya'aqub: your name shall not be called Ya'aqub any more, but YASHAR'AL shall be your name: and he called his name YASHAR'AL.
And 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH Dabar unto Ya'aqub, I AM 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH (AL'Mighty ONE): be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of you, and kings shall come out of your loins;
The land which I gave Abraham and Yachaq I give to you; and to your descendants after you I give this land.”
Then 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH went up from Ya'aqub in the place where He talked with him.
So Ya'aqub set up a pillar in the place where he talked with 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, a pillar of stone; and he poured a drink offering on it, and he poured oil on it.
And Ya'aqub called the name of the place where 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH spoke with him, Bathal.
Then they journeyed from Bathal. And when there was but a little distance to go to Aphrath, Rachal labored in childbirth, and she had hard labor.
Now it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said to her, “Do not fear; you will have this son also.”
And so it was, as her soul was departing (for she died), that she called his name Ban_uny; but his father called him Banyamyn.
So Rachal died and was buried on the way to Aphrath (that is, Bathlaham).
And Ya'aqub set a pillar on her grave, which is the pillar of Rachal’s grave to this day.
Then YASHAR'AL journeyed and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Adar.
And it happened, when YASHAR'AL dwelt in that land, that Rauban went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine; and YASHAR'AL heard about it. Now the sons of Ya'aqub were twelve:
The sons of La'ah were Rauban, Ya'aqub’s firstborn, and Simaun, Lauy, Yahudah, Issachar, and Zabulun;
The sons of Rachal were Ya'asaf and Banyamyn;
The sons of Bilhah, Rachal’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali;
And the sons of Zilpah, La'ah’s maidservant, were Gad and Ashar. These were the sons of Ya'aqub who were born to him in Padan Aram.
Then Ya'aqub came to his father Yachaq at Mamra, or Kirjath Arba (that is, Habrun), where Abraham and Yachaq had dwelt.
Now the days of Yachaq were one hundred and eighty years.
So Yachaq breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people, being old and full of days. And his sons Asau and Ya'aqub buried him.
Now this is the genealogy of Asau, who is Adum.
Asau took his wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah the daughter of Alun the Hittite; Ahulibamah the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibaun the Hibite;
And Basamath, Ishmaal’s daughter, sister of Nabayuth.
Now Adah bore Aliphaz to Asau, and Basamath bore Raual.
And Ahulibamah bore Yaush, Yaalam, and Kurah. These were the sons of Asau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Then Asau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the persons of his household, his cattle and all his animals, and all his goods which he had gained in the land of Canaan, and went to a country away from the presence of his brother Ya'aqub.
For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together, and the land where they were strangers could not support them because of their livestock.
So Asau dwelt in Mount Seir. Asau is Adum.
And this is the genealogy of Asau the father of the Adumites in Mount Sair.
These were the names of Asau’s sons: Aliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Asau, and Raual the son of Basamath the wife of Asau.
And the sons of Aliphaz were Taman, Umar, Zaphu, Gatam, and Kanaz.
Now Timna was the concubine of Aliphaz, Asau’s son, and she bore Amalak to Aliphaz. These were the sons of Adah, Asau’s wife.
These were the sons of Raual: Nahath, Zarah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These were the sons of Basamath, Asau’s wife.
These were the sons of Ahulibamah, Asau’s wife, the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibaun. And she bore to Asau: Yaush, Yaalam, and Kurah.
These were the chiefs of the sons of Asau. The sons of Aliphaz, the firstborn son of Asau, were Chief Taman, Chief Umar, Chief Zaphu, Chief Kanaz,
Chief Kurah, Chief Gatam, and Chief Amalak. These were the chiefs of Aliphaz in the land of Adum. They were the sons of Adah.
These were the sons of Raual, Asau’s son: Chief Nahath, Chief Zarah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. These were the chiefs of Raual in the land of Adum. These were the sons of Basamath, Asau’s wife.
And these were the sons of Ahulibamah, Asau’s wife: Chief Yaush, Chief Yaalam, and Chief Kurah. These were the chiefs who descended from Ahulibamah, Asau’s wife, the daughter of Anah.
These were the sons of Asau, who is Adum, and these were their chiefs.
These were the sons of Sair the Hurite who inhabited the land: Lutan, Shubal, Zibaun, Anah,
Dishun, Azar, and Dishan. These were the chiefs of the Hurites, the sons of Sair, in the land of Adum.
And the sons of Lutan were Huri and Hamam. Lutan’s sister was Timna.
These were the sons of Shubal: Alban, Manahath, Abal, Shaphu, and Unam.
These were the sons of Zibaun: both Ayah and Anah. This was the Anah who found the water in the wilderness as he pastured the donkeys of his father Zibaun.
These were the children of Anah: Dishun and Ahulibamah the daughter of Anah.
These were the sons of Dishun: Hamdan, Ashban, Ithran, and Charan.
These were the sons of Azar: Bilhan, Zaaban, and Akan.
These were the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These were the chiefs of the Hurites: Chief Lutan, Chief Shubal, Chief Zibaun, Chief Anah,
Chief Dishun, Chief Azar, and Chief Dishan. These were the chiefs of the Hurites, according to their chiefs in the land of Sair.
Now these were the kings who reigned in the land of Adum before any king reigned over the children of YASHAR'AL:
Bala the son of Baur reigned in Adum, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
And when Bala died, Yubab the son of Zarah of Buzrah reigned in his place.
When Yubab died, Husham of the land of the Tamanites reigned in his place.
And when Husham died, Hadad the son of Badad, who attacked Midian in the field of Muab, reigned in his place. And the name of his city was Abith.
When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrakah reigned in his place.
And when Samlah died, Shaul of Rahubuth-by-the-River reigned in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-Hanan the son of Achbur reigned in his place.
And when Baal-Hanan the son of Achbur died, Hadar reigned in his place; and the name of his city was Pau. His wife’s name was Mahatabal, the daughter of Matrad, the daughter of Mazahab.
And these were the names of the chiefs of Asau, according to their families and their places, by their names: Chief Timnah, Chief Albah, Chief Yathath,
Chief Ahulibamah, Chief Alah, Chief Pinun,
Chief Kanaz, Chief Taman, Chief Mibzar,
Chief Magdial, and Chief Iram. These were the chiefs of Adum, according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession. Asau was the father of the Adumites.
Now Ya'aqub dwelt in the land where his father was a stranger, in the land of Canaan.

This is the history of Ya'aqub and his family. Ya'asaf, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers. And the lad was with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives; and Ya'asaf brought a bad report of them to his father.
Now YASHAR'AL loved Ya'asaf more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a coat of many colors.
But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak with Shalum to him.
Now Ya'asaf had a dream, and he told it to his brothers; and they hated him even more.
So he said to them, “Please hear this dream which I have dreamed:
There we were, binding sheaves in the field. Then behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and indeed your sheaves stood all around and bowed down to my sheaf.”
And his brothers said to him, “Shall you indeed reign over us? Or shall you indeed have dominion over us?” So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.
Then Ya'asaf dreamed still another dream and told it to his brothers, and said, “Look, I have dreamed another dream. And this time, the sun, the moon, and the eleven stars bowed down to me.”

So he told it to his father and his brothers; and his father rebuked him and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall your mother and I and your brothers indeed come to bow down to the Arath (earth) before you?”
And his brothers envied him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
Then his brothers went to feed their father’s flock in Shacham.
And YASHAR'AL said to Ya'asaf, “Aren't your brothers feeding the flock in Shacham? Come, I will send you to them.” So Ya'asaf said to Ya'aqub, “Here I am.”
Then Ya'aqub said to Ya'asaf, “Please go and see if it is well with your brothers and the flocks, and bring back word to me.” So he sent him out of the Valley of Habrun, and he went to Shacham.
Now a certain man found Ya'asaf, and there he was, wandering in the field. And the man asked him, saying, “What are you seeking?”
So Ya'asaf said, “I am seeking my brothers. Please tell me where they are feeding their flocks.”
And the man said, “They have departed from here, for I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Duthan.’ ” So Ya'asaf went after his brothers and found them in Duthan.
Now when they saw him afar off, even before he came near them, they conspired against him to kill him.
Then they said to one another, “Look, this dreamer is coming!
Come therefore, let us now kill him and cast him into some pit; and we shall say, ‘Some wild beast has devoured him.’ We shall see what will become of his dreams!”
But Rauban heard it, and he delivered him out of their hands, and said, “Let us not kill him.”

And Rauban said to them, “Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit which is in the wilderness, and do not lay a hand on him”—that he might deliver him out of their hands, and bring him back to his father.
So it came to pass, when Ya'asaf had come to his brothers, that they stripped Ya'asaf of his coat, the coat of many colors that was on him.
Then they took Ya'asaf and cast him into a pit, for the pit was empty; there was no water in it.

And they sat down to eat a meal. Then they lifted their eyes and looked, and there was a company of Ishmaalites, coming from Gilaad with their camels, bearing spices, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry them down to Mitzraym.
So Yahudah said to his brothers, “What profit is there if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?
Come and let us sell him to the Ishmaalites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother and our flesh.” And his brothers listened.
Then the Midianite traders passed by; so the brothers pulled Ya'asaf up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaalites for twenty shekels of silver. And they took Ya'asaf to Mitzraym.
Then Rauban returned to the pit, and indeed Ya'asaf was not in the pit; and he tore his clothes.
And he returned to his brothers and said, “The lad is no more; and where shall I go?”
So they took Ya'asaf’s coat, killed a kid of the goats, and dipped the coat in the blood.
Then they brought the coat of many colors, to their father and said, “We have found this. Do you know whether it is your son’s coat or not?”
And he recognized it and said, “It is my son’s coat. A wild beast has devoured him. Without doubt Ya'asaf is torn to pieces.”
Then Ya'aqub tore his clothes, put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
And all his sons and all his daughters arose to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted, and he said, “For I shall go down into the grave to my son in mourning.” Thus his father wept for him.
Now the Midianites had sold Ya'asaf in Mitzraym to Putiphar, an officer of Phar'uh and captain of the guard.
It came to pass at that time that Yahudah departed from his brothers, and visited a certain Adullamite whose name was Hirah.
And Yahudah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua, and he married her and went in to her.
So she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Ar.
She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Unan.
And she conceived yet again and bore a son, and called his name Shalah. He was at Chazib when she bore him.
Then Yahudah took a wife for Ar his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Ar, Yahudah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, and 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH killed him.
And Yahudah said to Unan, “Go in to your brother’s wife and marry her, and raise up an heir to your brother.”
But Unan knew that the heir would not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in to his brother’s wife, that he emitted on the ground, lest he should give an heir to his brother.
And the thing which he did displeased 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH; therefore He killed Unan also.

Then Yahudah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house till my son Shalah is grown.” For he said, “Lest he also die like his brothers.” And Tamar went and dwelt in her father’s house.
Now in the process of time the daughter of Shua, Yahudah’s wife, died; and Yahudah was comforted, and went up to his sheepshearers at Timnah, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
And it was told Tamar, saying, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

So she took off her widow’s garments, covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself, and sat in an open place which was on the way to Timnah; for she saw that Shalah was grown, and she was not given to him as a wife.
When Yahudah saw her, he thought she was a harlot, because she had covered her face.
Then he turned to her by the way, and said, “Please let me come in to you”; for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. So she said, “What will you give me, that you may come in to me?”
And he said, “I will send a young goat from the flock.” So she said, “Will you give me a pledge till you send it?”
Then he said, “What pledge shall I give you?” So she said, “Your signet and cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” Then he gave them to her, and went in to her, and she was conceived by Yahudah.
So she arose and went away, and laid aside her veil and put on the garments of her widowhood.
And Yahudah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend the Adullamite, to receive his pledge from the woman’s hand, but he did not find her.
Then he asked the men of that place, saying, “Where is the harlot who was openly by the roadside?” And they said, “There was no harlot in this place.”
So he returned to Yahudah and said, “I cannot find her. Also, the men of the place said there was no harlot in this place.”
Then Yahudah said, “Let her take them for herself, lest we be shamed; for I sent this young goat and you have not found her.”

And it came to pass, about three months after, that Yahudah was told, saying, “Tamar your daughter-in-law has played the harlot; furthermore she is with child by harlotry.” So Yahudah said, “Bring her out and let her be burned!”
When she was brought out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying, “By the man to whom these belong, I am with child.” And she said, “Please determine whose these are—the signet and cord, and staff.”
So Yahudah acknowledged them and said, “She has been more righteous than I, because I did not give her to Shalah my son.” And he never knew her again.
Now it came to pass, at the time for giving birth, that behold, twins were in her womb.
And so it was, when she was giving birth, that the one put out his hand; and the midwife took a scarlet thread and bound it on his hand, saying, “This one came out first.”
Then it happened, as he drew back his hand, that his brother came out unexpectedly; and she said, “How did you break through? This breach be upon you!” Therefore his name was called Paraz.
Afterward his brother came out who had the scarlet thread on his hand. And his name was called Zarah.
Now Ya'asaf had been taken down to Mitzraym, and Putiphar an officer of Phar'uh, captain of the guard, a Mitzraym, bought him from the Ishmaalites who had taken him down there.
For 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was with Ya'asaf, and he was a successful man; and he was in the house of his master the Mitzraym.
And Ya'asaf master saw that 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was with him and that 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH made all Ya'asaf did to prosper in his hand.
So Ya'asaf found favor in Putiphar's sight, and served him. Then Putiphar made Ya'asaf overseer of his house, and all that he had he put under Ya'asaf's authority.

So it was, from the time that Putiphar had made Ya'asaf overseer of his house and all that he had, that 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH Baraked the Mitzraym's house for Ya'asaf sake; and the Barakah of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was on all that Putiphar had in the house and in the field.
Thus Putiphar left all that he had in Ya'asaf’s hand, and he did not know what he had except for the bread which he ate. Now Ya'asaf was handsome in form and appearance.
And it came to pass after these things that Putiphar’s wife cast longing eyes on Ya'asaf, and she said, “sleep with me.”
But Ya'asaf refused and said to his master’s wife, “Look, “my master trusts me with everything in his entire household.
No one here has more authority than I do. He has held back nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How could I do such a wicked thing? It would be a great sin against 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH.”
She kept putting pressure on Ya'asaf day after day, but he refused to sleep with her, and Ya'asaf kept out of her way as much as possible.
One day, however, no one else was around when Ya'asaf went into the house to do his work.

Then Putiphar's wife came and grabbed Ya'asaf by his cloak, demanding, “Come on, come sleep with me!” and Ya'asaf tore himself away, but he left his cloak in her hand as Ya'asaf ran out from the house.
And so it was, when she saw that Ya'asaf had left his garment in her hand and fled outside,

That she called to the men of her house and spoke to them, saying, “See, my master has brought in to us an Abarym (Hebrew) to mock us. For Ya'asaf came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice.
And it happened, when Ya'asaf heard that I lifted my voice and cried out, that he left his garment with me, and fled and went outside.”
So she kept his garment with her until his master came home.
Then she spoke to Putiphar with words like these, saying, “The Abarym (Hebrew) servant whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me;
So it happened, as I lifted my voice and cried out, that he left his garment with me and fled outside.”
So it was, when Ya'asaf master heard the words which his wife spoke to him, saying, “Your servant did to me after this manner,” that Putiphar's anger was aroused.
Then Putiphar took Ya'asaf and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were confined. And he was there in the prison.
But 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was with Ya'asaf and showed him kindness, and 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH gave Ya'asaf favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
And the keeper of the prison committed to Ya'asaf authority over all the prisoners who were in the prison; whatever they did there, it was Ya'asaf doing.
The keeper of the prison did not look into anything that was under Ya'asaf’s authority, because 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH was with him; and whatever Ya'asaf did, 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH made it prosper.
It came to pass after these things that the butler and the baker of the king of Mitzraym offended their master, the king of Mitzraym.
And Phar'uh was angry with his two officers, the chief butler and the chief baker.
So he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison, the place where Ya'asaf was confined.
And the captain of the guard charged Ya'asaf with them, and he served them; so they were in custody for a while.
Then the butler and the baker of the king of Mitzraym, who were confined in the prison, had a dream, both of them, each man’s dream in one night and each man’s dream with its own interpretation.
And Ya'asaf came in to them in the morning and looked at them, and saw that they were sad.
So Ya'asaf asked Pharauh’s officers who were with him in the custody of his master’s house, saying, “Why do you look so sad today?”
And they said to him, “We each have had a dream, and there is no interpreter of it.” So Ya'asaf said to them, “all interpretations belong to 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH? Tell me your dreams, please.”
Then the chief butler told his dream to Ya'asaf, and said to him, “Behold, in my dream a vine was before me,
and in the vine were three branches; it was as though it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and its clusters brought forth ripe grapes.
Then Phar'uh’s cup was in my hand; and I took the grapes and pressed them into Phar'uh’s cup, and placed the cup in Phar'uh’s hand.”
And Ya'asaf said to him, “This is the interpretation of your dream: The three branches are three days.
Now within three days Phar'uh will lift up your head and restore you to your place, and you will put Phar'uh’s cup in his hand according to the former manner, when you were his butler.
But remember me when it is well with you, and please show kindness to me; make mention of me to Phar'uh, and get me out of this prison.
For indeed I was stolen away from the land of the Abarym (Hebrews); and also I have done nothing here that they should put me into the dungeon.”
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said to Ya'asaf, “I also was in my dream, and there were three white baskets on my head.
In the uppermost basket were all kinds of baked goods for Phar'uh, and the birds ate them out of the basket on my head.”
So Ya'asaf answered and said, “This is the interpretation of it: The three baskets are three days.
Within three days Phar'uh will lift off your head from you and hang you on a tree; and the birds will eat your flesh from you.”
Now it came to pass on the third day, which was Phar'uh’s birthday, that he made a feast for all his servants; and he lifted up the head of the chief butler and of the chief baker among his servants.
Then he restored the chief butler to his butlership again, and he placed the cup in Phar'uh’s hand.
But he hanged the chief baker, as Ya'asaf had interpreted to them.
Yet the chief butler did not remember Ya'asaf, but forgot him.
Then it came to pass, at the end of two full years, that Phar'uh had a dream; and behold, he stood by the river.
In his dream he saw seven fat, healthy cows come up out of the river and begin grazing in the marsh grass.
Then he saw seven more cows come up behind them from the Nile, but these were scrawny and thin. These cows stood beside the fat cows on the riverbank.
And the ugly and gaunt cows ate up the seven fine looking and fat cows. So Phar'uh awoke.
He slept and dreamed a second time; and suddenly seven heads of grain came up on one stalk, plump and good.
Then seven more heads of grain appeared, but these were shriveled and withered by the east wind.
And these thin heads swallowed up the seven plump, well-formed heads! Then Phar'uh woke up again and realized it was a dream.

The next morning Pharauh was very disturbed by the dreams. So he called for all the magicians and wise men of Mitzraym. When Phar'uh told them his dreams, not one of them could tell him what the dreams meant.
Finally, Phar'uh’s chief cup-bearer spoke up. “Today I have been reminded of my failure,” he told Phar'uh.
“Some time ago, you were angry with the chief baker and me, and you imprisoned us in the palace of the captain of the guard.
One night the chief baker and I each had a dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
There was a young Abarym (Hebrew) man with us in the prison who was a slave of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he told us what each of our dreams meant.
And everything happened just as he had predicted. I was restored to my position as cup-bearer, and the chief baker was executed and impaled on a pole.”
Phar'uh sent for Ya'asaf at once, and he was quickly brought from the prison. After they shaved him and changed his clothes, he went in and stood before Phar'uh.
Then Phar'uh said to Ya'asaf, “I had a dream last night, and no one here can tell me what it means. But I have heard that when you hear about a dream you can interpret it.”
“It is beyond my power to do this,” Ya'asaf replied. “But 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH can tell you what it means and set you at ease.”
So Phar'uh told Ya'asaf his dream. “In my dream,” he said, “I was standing on the bank of the Nile River,
And I saw seven fat, healthy cows come up out of the river and begin grazing in the marsh grass.
But then I saw seven sick-looking cows, scrawny and thin, come up after them. I have never seen such sorry-looking animals in all the land of Mitzraym.
These thin, scrawny cows ate the seven fat cows.
But afterward you wouldn’t have known it, for they were still as thin and scrawny as before! Then I woke up.
“I dreamt again and I also saw seven heads of grain, full and beautiful, growing on a single stalk.
Then seven more heads of grain appeared, but these were blighted, shriveled, and withered by the east wind.
And the shriveled heads swallowed the seven healthy heads. I told these dreams to the magicians, but no one could tell me what they mean.”
Ya'asaf responded, “Both of Phar'uh’s dreams mean the same thing. 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH is telling Phar'uh in advance what HE is about to do.
The seven healthy cows and the seven healthy heads of grain both represent seven years of prosperity.
The seven thin, scrawny cows that came up later and the seven thin heads of grain, withered by the east wind, represent seven years of famine.
“This will happen just as I have described it, for 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has revealed to Phar'uh in advance what He is about to do.
The next seven years will be a period of great prosperity throughout the land of Mitzraym.
But afterward there will be seven years of famine so great that all the prosperity will be forgotten in Mitzraym. Famine will destroy the land.
This famine will be so severe that even the memory of the good years will be erased.
As for having two similar dreams, it means that these events have been decreed by 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH, and HE will soon make them happen.
“Therefore, Phar'uh should find an intelligent and wise man and put him in charge of the entire land of Mitzraym.
Then Phar'uh should appoint supervisors over the land and let them collect one-fifth of all the crops during the seven good years.
Have them gather all the food produced in the good years that are just ahead and bring it to Phar'uh’s storehouses. Store it away, and guard it so there will be food in the cities.
That way there will be enough to eat when the seven years of famine come to the land of Mitzraym. Otherwise this famine will destroy the land.”
Ya'asaf’s suggestions were well received by Phar'uh and his officials.
So Phar'uh asked his officials, “Can we find anyone else like this man so obviously filled with the Ruach of 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH?”
Then Phar'uh said to Ya'asaf, “Since 𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has revealed the meaning of the dreams to you, clearly no one else is as intelligent or wise as you are.
You will be in charge of my court, and all my people will take orders from you. Only I, sitting on my throne, will have a rank higher than yours.”
Phar'uh said to Ya'asaf, “I hereby put you in charge of the entire land of Mitzraym.”
Then Phar'uh removed his signet ring from his hand and placed it on Ya'asaf’s finger. He dressed him in fine linen clothing and hung a gold chain around his neck.
Then he had Ya'asaf ride in the chariot reserved for his second-in-command. And wherever Ya'asaf went, the command was shouted, “Kneel down!” So Phar'uh put Ya'asaf in charge of all Mitzraym.
And Phar'uh said to Ya'asaf, “I am Phar'uh, but no one will lift a hand or foot in the entire land of Mitzraym without your approval.”

Then Phar'uh gave Ya'asaf a new Mitzraym name, Zaphanath-panaah. He also gave him a wife, whose name was Asanath. She was the daughter of Putiphara, the priest of Un. So Ya'asaf took charge of the entire land of Mitzraym.
Ya'asaf was thirty years old when he began serving in the court of Pharauh, the king of Mitzraym. And when Ya'asaf left Phar'uh’s presence, he inspected the entire land of Mitzraym.
As predicted, for seven years the land produced bumper crops.
During those years, Ya'asaf gathered all the crops grown in Mitzraym and stored the grain from the surrounding fields in the cities.
He piled up huge amounts of grain like sand on the seashore. Finally, he stopped keeping records because there was too much to measure.
During this time, before the first of the famine years, two sons were born to Ya'asaf and his wife, Asanath, the daughter of Putiphara, the priest of Un.
Ya'asaf named his older son Manassah, for he said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has made me forget all my troubles and everyone in my father’s family.”
Ya'asaf named his second son Aphraim, for he said, “𐤀𐤋𐤅𐤄_ALUAH has made me fruitful in this land of my grief.”
At last the seven years of bumper crops throughout the land of Mitzraym came to an end.
Then the seven years of famine began, just as Ya'asaf had predicted. The famine also struck all the surrounding countries, but throughout Mitzraym there was plenty of food.
Eventually, the famine spread throughout the land of Mitzraym as well. And when the people cried out to Pharauh for food, he told them, “Go to Ya'asaf, and do whatever he tells you.”
So with severe famine everywhere, Ya'asaf opened up the storehouses and distributed grain to all of Mitzraym, for the famine was severe throughout the land of Mitzraym.
